svg.title: MAPP backend: layered monolith today, modular monolith target
svg.desc: On the left, today's layered monolith: handler, service and store layers cut across 27 business areas that all share one stores registry, one generated sqlcdb package and one migrations folder. On the right, the modular monolith as built: a kernel of platform packages, then 27 modules in five tiers, each publishing its contract in its root package and keeping its service, store, handler, queries and generated code in a compiler-private internal folder, owning its tables and wired together by the composition root.
svg.text: MAPP backend — from layered monolith to modular monolith
One binary, one database, one transaction throughout. 27 business areas · 59 cross-module imports · no cycles · 5 tiers. Built (ADR-0022).
BEFORE — layered monolith (ADR-0003)
The layer is the first thing you see; the module is a folder convention.
Handler layer — Gin
286 routes registered across 27 areas
Service layer — every business rule
59 cross-module imports live here; types of other modules cross freely
Store layer
store.go + store_postgres.go per area
Shared by every module — the coupling that remains
internal/stores · one stores.Set holding all 27 stores
one generated sqlcdb package · any module may call any table's queries
one migrations folder · one queries folder · no table has an owner
The four gaps
1 · Behaviour is inverted (deps.go interfaces), but the provider's types still cross.
2 · The data layer is shared; stores.PlanStore exists for other modules.
3 · No module owns its tables.
4 · Nothing enforces any of it — internal/ is used once, at the repo root.
Already true: the graph is a DAG, no cycles, and 27 of 32 query files
touch only their own module's tables.
NOW — modular monolith (ADR-0022)
The module is the unit; the layering lives inside it, unchanged.
internal/app — composition root
builds each module in order, fills its ports from other contracts, mounts its routes
internal/modules/plan/ — every module has these parts
plan.go — the published contract
types, ports and constructors as aliases — the only part others import
internal/ — private, enforced by the Go compiler
core/ (model · store · service · handler) · queries/ · sqlcdb/ (generated)
unreachable from any other module — no linter needed
its tables — one owner; others read its views
plantest/ — its in-memory fake
Tiers, computed from the imports the code has today
KERNEL
platform/* only — no business rule; migrations stay in one folder
TIER 0–1
history · widgetdata · spa · people · settings · access · overspend · rollup · financials · bulk · swbs · sample
TIER 2
plan · campaign · lineitem · approval · budget · allwork · auth · home · customdashboard · dataset
TIER 3
activity · purchaserequest · workbook
TIER 4
dashboard · simulatedgsap — pure consumers, nothing depends on them
A module may import the kernel and any lower tier — never its own tier or higher.
All 27 modules sit behind their contract; 13 have fan-in zero.
How modules talk — synchronous, in one transaction
A asks B — A declares the interface it needs; internal/app fills it from b.go.
A reacts to B — B publishes a hook; the composition root subscribes A to it.
A needs many of B's rows — B publishes a read-only SQL view, named in its contract.
Both need the same sum — a shared domain module (rollup), never the kernel.
No queue, no event bus, no eventual consistency. The hook pattern already exists:
deleting a team already removes dashboard and dataset shares in the same transaction.
Enforced by: the compiler · depguard · eleven architecture tests.
Migration — seven stages, done (stage 4 dropped)
1 ✓ The module map, the allow-list and the architecture tests.
2 ✓ spa moved behind its contract — the pilot.
3 ✓ The 12 other fan-in-zero modules moved.
4 — platform/ → kernel/ dropped: platform/ is the kernel (D-380).
5 ✓ The other 14 moved; history publishes a narrow Recorder.
6 ✓ Per-module sqlc · table owners · 3 views · overspend declared.
7 ✓ Only internal/app builds modules; stores.Set is wiring only.
Each move kept the tree green: build, tests, architecture tests.
What does not change
One binary, one PostgreSQL database, one transaction — no service split, no network hop, no distributed transaction. The Azure design (ADR-0021) is unaffected.
The API contract: 286 endpoints, the same paths and error envelope; openapi.yaml stays the source of truth and the contract tests pass unchanged.
Access control: the fail-closed route table and scoped service checks are untouched. The layering: handler → service → store, per module, exactly as ADR-0003 describes.
The frontend is already feature-sliced with ESLint enforcing inward dependencies — this brings the backend level with it.
